input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-518: Collaborative Seminar in Computer Graphics. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Computer Graphics. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Computer Graphics and Visualization cluster. Enrollment in this course requires permission from the department offering the course. Contact Hours: Laboratory 3, Lecture 2

Source excerpts:

[khronos-opengl]
The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.

[mit-computer-graphics]
Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.

Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Computer Graphics and Visualization cluster. Enrollment in this course requires permission from the department offering the course. beats.claim: The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages.
beats.example: Vertex data enters the pipeline first, where vertex shaders modify position, color, or normal attributes before downstream stages.
beats.title: Pipeline Foundation
beats.visualDirection: Display a left-to-right flowchart showing vertex input → vertex shader → primitive assembly → clipping → rasterization → fragment shader → framebuffer.

beats.claim: Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles.
beats.example: Three connected vertices form a triangle primitive, which the pipeline then processes as a single geometric unit for rendering.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly
beats.visualDirection: Show a wireframe triangle with labeled vertices, highlighting how three points are bound into a single primitive before clipping.

beats.claim: Clipping removes portions outside the view volume.
beats.example: A triangle extending beyond the camera's frustum is sliced at the clipping plane boundaries, discarding the exterior segments.
beats.title: Clipping Stage
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a 3D cube partially outside a transparent viewing box, with clipped edges highlighted in red and retained portions in blue.

beats.claim: Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates.
beats.example: Each triangle is subdivided into pixel-aligned fragments, with each fragment receiving interpolated attributes for downstream processing.
beats.title: Rasterization
beats.visualDirection: Render a grid overlay on a triangle, showing how each pixel cell becomes a fragment candidate with assigned vertex attributes.

beats.claim: Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs.
beats.example: Color and normal values are linearly interpolated across a triangle's pixels using barycentric coordinates to ensure smooth shading.
beats.title: Interpolation
beats.visualDirection: Display a color gradient across a triangle, with interpolation weights labeled at each vertex and midpoint to show value distribution.

beats.claim: Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations.
beats.example: Fragment shaders evaluate lighting equations and material properties to generate final color and alpha values for each pixel.
beats.title: Fragment Processing
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of a raw triangle mesh and its shaded output, with a callout box explaining the fragment shader's role.

beats.claim: Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values.
beats.example: Each fragment's depth value is compared against the depth buffer; fragments with greater depth are discarded to maintain correct occlusion.
beats.title: Depth Testing
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate two overlapping triangles with depth values, highlighting the front triangle as retained and the back triangle as rejected by depth testing.

beats.claim: Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value.
beats.example: Translucent surfaces blend the new fragment's color with the underlying color using alpha values to produce semi-transparent overlays.
beats.title: Blending
beats.visualDirection: Render a semi-transparent square over a solid background, with a legend showing the blending equation and resulting composite color.

beats.claim: Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.
beats.example: Explicitly defining vertex, fragment, and texture coordinate spaces prevents misalignment during sampling and ensures consistent precision across pipeline stages.
beats.title: Coordinate Spaces
beats.visualDirection: Display a diagram of three nested coordinate spaces (world, view, clip) with labeled axes, emphasizing explicit mapping between them.

beats.claim: Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.
beats.example: Instructor-led review checks that coordinate mappings are explicit, sampling rates match resolution requirements, and error bounds remain within acceptable thresholds.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with four boxes: explicit conventions, sampling decisions, measurable error, and coordinate space alignment, each with a tick mark for verification.

learningObjectives: Define the standard stages of the OpenGL graphics pipeline and their sequential processing order.
Explain how geometric transformations and viewing models map 3D scene data to a 2D pixel grid.
Evaluate visual correctness by identifying how sampling decisions, shading models, and coordinate spaces impact rendering outcomes.

input.text: Stress-test the reasoning around Depth Testing with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Consider this worked case: Each fragment's depth value is compared against the depth buffer; fragments with greater depth are discarded to maintain correct occlusion. On screen, illustrate two overlapping triangles with depth values, highlighting the front triangle as retained and the back triangle as rejected by depth testing. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

Apply Interpolation to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Consider this worked case: Color and normal values are linearly interpolated across a triangle's pixels using barycentric coordinates to ensure smooth shading. On screen, display a color gradient across a triangle, with interpolation weights labeled at each vertex and midpoint to show value distribution. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

Next, compare the choices involved in Rasterization and make the decision criteria explicit. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Consider this worked case: Each triangle is subdivided into pixel-aligned fragments, with each fragment receiving interpolated attributes for downstream processing. On screen, render a grid overlay on a triangle, showing how each pixel cell becomes a fragment candidate with assigned vertex attributes. With the foundation in place, examine how Clipping Stage operates in a concrete sequence. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Consider this worked case: A triangle extending beyond the camera's frustum is sliced at the clipping plane boundaries, discarding the exterior segments. On screen, illustrate a 3D cube partially outside a transparent viewing box, with clipped edges highlighted in red and retained portions in blue. Consider this worked case: Vertex data enters the pipeline first, where vertex shaders modify position, color, or normal attributes before downstream stages. On screen, display a left-to-right flowchart showing vertex input → vertex shader → primitive assembly → clipping → rasterization → fragment shader → framebuffer. Now define Primitive Assembly precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles.
